months.headline: ISRO’s LVM3‑M6 launch on Dec 24 delivered the heaviest satellite from Indian soil, cementing its commercial launch capability and heralding a new era of public‑private space initiatives.

points.text: ISRO confirmed and executed the LVM3‑M6 mission on Dec 24, 2025, using the heavy‑lift LVM3 (Bahubali) from the second launch pad at Satish Dhawan Space Centre, marking the launch of the heaviest satellite ever deployed from Indian soil.

The mission carried the U.S. commercial satellite “Bluebird Block‑2” (also called “Bluebird‑6”) under a contract with NewSpace India Limited, highlighting ISRO’s expanding role in the global commercial launch market.

India launched a $145 million public‑private Earth‑observation partnership led by Pixxel, involving firms like Satsure, Dhruva Space, and Piersight, signalling a strategic shift toward leveraging space data for agriculture and industry.
The successful heavy‑lift launch was framed as part of ISRO’s broader 2026 roadmap, which includes crewed lunar flybys and Mars test flights, underscoring its rising stature in the global space race.

months.why_it_matters: The launch demonstrates ISRO’s growing technical capability and commercial credibility, while the new Earth‑observation partnership expands the economic impact of space technology in India. Together, they position India as a key player in the upcoming era of lunar and interplanetary exploration.

months.headline: ISRO kicked off 2026 with the PSLV‑C62 launch, unveiling an advanced Earth‑observation satellite and multiple co‑passenger payloads while outlining a human‑spaceflight roadmap.

points.text: ISRO launched PSLV‑C62 on Jan 12, deploying the EOS‑N1 advanced Earth‑observation satellite and 15 co‑passenger satellites, including eight from foreign partners.
The launch marked the start of India’s 2026 space calendar, showcasing ISRO’s capability to conduct multi‑payload missions and reaffirming its role in global satellite deployment.
Former ISRO director Josyula A. Kamalakar outlined an ambitious roadmap for sustained human spaceflight, indicating the agency’s long‑term strategic vision beyond satellite launches.
A Google Republic Day doodle highlighted ISRO, reflecting national pride and governmental emphasis on space as a pillar of the ‘Viksit Bharat’ development agenda.

months.why_it_matters: The PSLV‑C62 mission demonstrates ISRO’s operational strength and international collaboration, while the articulated human‑spaceflight roadmap signals a shift toward more ambitious exploration goals; public recognition underscores space’s central role in India’s development narrative.

months.headline: ISRO pushes forward with Chandrayaan‑4 and Gaganyaan plans while a former employee is arrested for alleged murder

points.text: The agency identified a south‑polar lunar landing site and received government approval for the Chandrayaan‑4 sample‑return mission, which is now slated for at least two years out.
Astronauts selected for the Gaganyaan crew are applying lessons from prior Russian and U.S. training programs as India prepares for its maiden human spaceflight scheduled for 2027.
A former ISRO employee, Nagesh Ishwar Rao, was arrested and taken into custody after being accused of strangling his wife to death in Bengaluru.

months.why_it_matters: The lunar and human‑spaceflight initiatives underscore India's expanding role in deep‑space exploration, while the criminal case highlights the need for vigilance regarding the welfare and conduct of agency personnel.

months.headline: ISRO pushes forward with defense satellite plans, orbital docking tests, and new commercial ties despite NavIC setbacks

points.text: India’s navigation satellite system (NavIC) was reported as not fully functional, raising concerns that the country may be unable to use it for security and strategic purposes.
ISRO and the Ministry of Defence are developing a plan to launch specialised satellites dedicated to protecting India’s assets in orbit.
The agency is preparing two advanced orbital docking experiments, Spadex‑2 and Spadex‑3, as stepping stones toward the long‑term goal of operating the Bharatiya Antariksha Station.

Eutelsat entered talks with ISRO to secure future satellite launch partnerships, aiming to reduce reliance on SpaceX and Ariane rockets, while India’s private space sector gained a new contender in Bharath Space Vehicle, founded by veteran ISRO scientists.

months.why_it_matters: These developments show ISRO balancing critical national security needs, ambitious human‑spaceflight goals, and growing commercial collaborations, all while addressing the strategic gap caused by NavIC’s limited functionality.

months.headline: ISRO advances crewed mission tests and data access while facing internal security controversy

points.text: The agency completed its second integrated air‑drop test (IADT‑02) for the Gaganyaan human spaceflight programme, marking another key milestone toward crewed launch capability.

The agency opened a call for proposals to use data from its Aditya‑L1 solar mission, expanding scientific research opportunities, even as a former scientist’s allegations of a spy network and missile‑technology leaks sparked a security controversy.

months.why_it_matters: These developments move India closer to achieving its first crewed spaceflight and enhance climate and solar research, while the security allegations could impact ISRO's reputation and international collaborations.

months.headline: May 2026: India’s security, education, and diplomatic moves set the backdrop for ISRO’s steady month

points.text: India carried out Operation Sindoor, a high‑precision cross‑border counter‑terrorism strike that marks a shift in its security doctrine, potentially influencing ISRO’s dual‑use technology priorities.

The cancellation of the NEET‑UG 2026 exam and a parliamentary committee’s endorsement of pen‑and‑paper testing sparked debate over India’s education system, highlighting challenges in nurturing scientific talent crucial for ISRO’s workforce.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi reiterated India’s support for a rules‑based international order in Ukraine and West Asia, a stance that could affect ISRO’s diplomatic engagements and launch service agreements.

A low‑pressure system in the Bay of Bengal and the Blue Origin Glenn rocket explosion underscored both domestic weather challenges and global space‑industry turbulence, factors that shape ISRO’s launch scheduling and competitive landscape.

months.why_it_matters: These developments influence ISRO’s strategic priorities, talent pipeline, and operational environment, even as the agency itself reported no major launches or announcements.

data.arc: India’s space narrative kicked off in June 2025 with its first commercial astronaut flying to the ISS, establishing a new human‑spaceflight foothold. Over the summer, ISRO cemented international collaboration by launching the joint US‑India NISAR satellite and confirmed the first Gaganyaan test flight for December, while also rolling out indigenous technologies such as the Vikram microprocessor. The latter half of 2025 saw a shift toward commercial and industrial integration, highlighted by the transfer of PSLV development to Indian industry, a heavy‑lift LVM3‑M6 launch of the world’s heaviest satellite from Indian soil, and a $145 million public‑private Earth‑observation partnership. Entering 2026, ISRO expanded its multi‑payload capabilities with PSLV‑C62, outlined an ambitious human‑spaceflight roadmap, and advanced lunar and orbital docking projects, even as it grappled with NavIC functionality issues and a security controversy. The program now balances crewed missions, lunar exploration, defense satellites, and growing commercial launch services, positioning India as a rising contender in the global space race.

turning_points.why: India’s first commercial astronaut launched on Axiom‑4, marking the nation’s entry into crewed spaceflight on a private vehicle.
ISRO confirmed the first Gaganyaan test flight for December, moving the human spaceflight program from planning to execution.
The agency transferred 50% of PSLV development to Indian industry and inaugurated the Infinity Campus, signaling a major shift toward public‑private manufacturing.
LVM3‑M6 delivered the heaviest satellite from Indian soil and launched a $145 million public‑private Earth‑observation partnership, showcasing ISRO’s expanding commercial launch capability.
NavIC was reported as not fully functional, prompting defense satellite plans and highlighting vulnerabilities in India’s navigation system.
